excerpt: === README.md (md) === # MEJO570-DDJ-Fall2019 Material for Data Driven Journalism, Fall 2019 === intro2ggplot-politics-s2.Rmd (rmd) === --- title: "GGPLOT ENRS" output: html_document: df_print: paged --- Import the libraries. ```{r} library(tidyverse) ``` We're going to start with our results2018 dataframe and then create a list of just candidates for the N.C. state House. OK, so let's get just the state House races. ```{r} NCHouse2018 <- results2018 %>% filter( str_detect(contest_name,"NC HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES*") ) %>% group_by(contest_name, choice, choice_party) %>% summarize(Votes=sum(total_votes)) ``` ```{r} ggplot( NCHouse2018 ) + geom_col( mapping = aes(x=choice, y=Votes) ) ``` What is "geom_col" ? ```{r} ?geom_col ``` Anyway, that chart is pretty useless. Let's just look at one contest. ```{r} NCHouse2018 %>% filter(contest_name == "NC HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES DISTRICT 003") %>% ggplot() + #we don't need to use the dataframe as the argument here beacuse we are piping it in from the first line in this R statement geom_col( mapping = aes(x=choice, y=Votes) ) ``` But if you want to put it in order, you need to use the reorder() function in the value you assign to the x-axis. ```{r} NCHouse2018 %>% filter(contest_name == "NC HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES DISTRICT 003") %>% ggplot() + #we don't need to use the dataframe as the argument here beacuse we are piping it from the first line in this R statement geom_col( mapping = aes(x=reorder(choice, Votes), y=Votes) ) ``` Least to most probably makes more sense to folks. So put a minus sign before the field you want to order by. ```{r} NCHouse2018 %>% filter(contest_name == "NC HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES DISTRICT 003") %>% ggplot() + #we don't need to use the dataframe as the argument here beacuse we are piping it in from the first line in the R statement geom_col( mapping = aes(x=reorder(choice, -Votes), y=Votes) ) ``` Now let's change to a different question.... Did one party have a lot more candidates running? (For example, in unopposed races?) To graph the number of candidates from each party we can switch from the geom_col() function to the geom_bar(). The geom_bar() function by default does a count of the number of rows in each category for whatever field you select. So let's look at the party of each candidate, which in this dataset is the column called `"choice Party". ```{r} ggplot(data = NCHouse2018) + geom_bar(mapping = aes(x=choice_party)) ``` OK, but what if you want to just focus on that relatively small difference between Democratic and Republican candidates? We can filter the data right here inside ggplot. ```{r} ggplot( data = filter(NCHouse2018, choice_party %in% # we are using %in% because we are looking for more than one value in the same column. c("DEM", "REP") ) ) + geom_bar( mapping = aes( x=choice_party ) ) ``` Hmmm.. maybe it would be easier to see when expressed as a percentage... What about looking at what percentage of all candidates that are in each party? You can explicitly turn the y axis of a bar chart into proportions using "y=..prop.." and "group=1" (Why? Because I said so...?)
